title: The morning adhkar
tomorrow: the espresso machine hisses, the rush is on. who stops at noon?

lines: DADI ON THE PORCH, IN THE DARK.
cards: Plenty of phones get checked before feet touch the floor. Amira's Dadi has a different first five minutes.
After Fajr she sits on the porch in the dark with her tea and says the same words she says every morning, some of them three times over. Those are the morning adhkar, the remembrances.
And in Amira's house they've started a small argument: Amira says hers on the bus, well after sunrise. Dadi says that's too late. Two real views, both inside the tradition.

teach.b: First, what's being said. Adhkar is the plural of dhikr, remembrance. One, kept in Sahih Muslim, begins: we have entered the morning, and the whole dominion has entered it too, belonging to God.
Another, in Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi, is said three times: in the name of God, with whose name nothing on earth or in heaven can harm.

The Qur'an gives the reason in Pickthall's words: "Remember Allah with much remembrance. And glorify Him early and late." Now the two views. Dadi's: the morning adhkar belong between Fajr and sunrise.
The Qur'an pairs glorifying God with the time before the sun rises, and those dark minutes are the seam between night and day, before anything else has claimed you.
Say them then, and they open the day instead of interrupting it.
Amira's, and some scholars hold it too: morning in Arabic runs past sunrise into the forenoon, and the reports say only "when you reach the morning".
So the window is wider, and a person on an early bus or a dawn shift is still inside it.
Both agree on more than they argue about. The words are the same. And both would rather you say them late than skip them.

how: After Fajr, Muslims who keep the morning adhkar recite set remembrances from the hadith, some once and some three times, often from a small booklet or from memory; scholars differ on whether the window ends at sunrise or runs through the forenoon.

o: a long sermon given at the mosque every morning
remembrances of God said after Fajr to open the day
the dawn prayer itself, said before the sun comes up

games.q: what's inside the morning — tap the pairs.
p: when the Qur'an says to glorify God
in the name of God, nothing can harm

s: the morning adhkar are a single fixed prayer said once
they're a set of remembrances from the hadith, some said once and some three times.
scholars agree the window closes exactly at sunrise
some hold it ends at sunrise; others read morning as running into the forenoon.
the Qur'an tells believers to glorify God early and late
33:42, in Pickthall's words: glorify Him early and late.

games.q: you've always heard the morning adhkar only count before sunrise. state the wider view at its strongest.
o: the time never matters; any hour of the day can be morning.
morning in Arabic runs into the forenoon, and the reports only say when you reach the morning.
the adhkar are optional anyway, so the window doesn't matter.
games.why: the wider view's best case is the language and the reports themselves. the other view's best case is the Qur'an's 'before the rising of the sun'. both say the same words.

practice: Take a scrap of paper and write one morning line by hand, slowly. If it's yours, the line from Sahih Muslim: we have entered the morning, and the dominion belongs to God.
If it isn't, one plain sentence naming what this morning has already given you. Then rest your hand on it while the time runs.

wordCard.voice: The morning adhkar: remembrances said after Fajr, some of them three times, to open the day with God's name before anything else does.

orig.note: Arabic: the remembrances of the morning; adhkar is the plural of dhikr.

carryVoice: Something for the bus ride: morning, remembered, before the day starts talking. Two views, the same words.

sources.q: Remember Allah with much remembrance. And glorify Him early and late.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 2723 (we have entered the morning, and the dominion belongs to God)
Sunan Abu Dawud 5088; Jami' al-Tirmidhi 3388 (in the name of God, with whose name nothing harms, three times)
Qur'an 20:130; 50:39 (glorify before the rising of the sun)
